input.body:
Archive note. Technical scope only, per the March 16 retro convention (deploy discipline, not a broad postmortem).

Summary
- Date / trigger: March 15, 2023, ~5:30 PM Pacific. Small deploy — roughly a ten-line change — with a disproportionately large blast radius.
- Duration: ~18 hours end-to-end.
- Surface symptom: spike in API HTTP 500 errors.
- Status by March 16: service restored, obvious rough edges resolved.

Mechanism (the technical chain)
1. A narrow code change altered behavior around the entitlement-check path.
2. Under certain conditions, that path fell back to a branch that did not behave correctly — specifically, a fallback that the rest of the system treated as a transient failure.
3. Because the fallback signaled "try again," retries piled up in the worker pool. Each retried request could itself re-enter the fallback, compounding the load.
4. The worker pool saturated. Newly arriving work could not be scheduled promptly, and the API surface started returning HTTP 500s as requests timed out waiting for capacity.
5. Once the offending change was identified and rolled back (or the fallback corrected), the retry pile drained, the pool returned to normal, and the 500 rate fell back to baseline.

Why the impact was uneven across tenants
The user-facing question this archive is meant to answer is not "was there an outage" — it is "why did some tenants feel it sharply while others barely noticed." The asymmetry follows directly from the mechanism:

- Entitlements are per-tenant. Any code path that misbehaves on entitlement checks will exercise unevenly, because the population of entitlements being checked at any moment is itself uneven — tenants vary in workspace size, number of connected sources, sync cadence, and how recently their data was refreshed.
- Retry storms amplify per-tenant load. A tenant whose traffic happens to be flowing through the changed code path at higher volume, or whose checks are landing on the inputs that trigger the fallback, contributes disproportionately to the retry pile. Tenants whose traffic bypasses the path see no degradation.
- Idempotency matters. Tenants whose requests were idempotent could absorb a retry safely; tenants whose downstream effects were not idempotent saw more visible breakage from the same retry volume.
- Timing of the pile-up matters more than absolute traffic. Tenants whose requests landed while the worker pool was already saturated waited; tenants whose requests landed early or late in the window cleared. The 18-hour window is long enough that the population of "currently affected" tenants shifted throughout the incident.

In short: the blast radius was wide because the worker pool is shared, but the per-tenant experience was determined by which tenants' traffic intersected the broken entitlement-check fallback, and when.

What this archive deliberately does not contain
- The literal diff of the ten-line change.
- A named list of affected tenants or customer-facing communications.
- A timeline with named responders (other than noting Devon was the trace lead).
- Action items or follow-ups — those belong to the deploy-discipline retro, not this note.

COMPASS v0.1 — TUESDAY WORKING SESSION
Date:     Tue 2025-01-21, HH:MM–HH:MM PT (Sarah to send)
Chair:    Morgan
In room:  Anna, Nadia, Jake, Leo, Sarah

BOUNDARY (read at top, do not relitigate)
- No board dashboard. No new hiring lane off a single-customer signal.
- Atlas touchpoints route via support/product. No founder-direct.

- Mercury activation leads; Evergreen stays current-state / procurement.

FRAME — each signal answers FIVE questions, no more
  1. Action — what this signal triggers (or explicitly doesn't).
  2. Audience — who sees it; who does not.
  3. Evidence + caveat — what travels with the signal; the caveat that kills over-reading.
  4. Account-note / source-quality floor — what must be true on the CRM note before the signal is publishable.
  5. Not building — what Compass v0.1 explicitly does not do as a result of this signal.

SIGNAL SLOTS — name the signal, then run the five:
  A. ____________________________
  B. ____________________________
  C. ____________________________
  D. ____________________________   (cap at 4; merge or drop if we run short)

CLOSING TEST — any signal that fails goes back to Morgan/Devon, NOT the room:
  - Publishing this requires a board-facing view? -> no.
  - Acting on this implies a new hire? -> no.
  - Acting on this binds a roadmap date or scope? -> no.

ADMIN — Sarah: invite title "Compass v0.1 signal review (Anna, Nadia, Jake, Leo)" — descriptive, not "sync". Hold 45 min. Confirm Mon EOD.

- Source of the original frame: Morgan's 2025-01-20 prompt, asking for a compact working-session agenda with the 5-question frame and the no-board-dashboard / no-new-hiring-lane boundary explicit.

[2024-03-22T09:06:00-07:00] HR’s finalist packet for Nadia is here.

From: HR
To: Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes
Cc: Sarah Kim
Date: Fri, Mar 22, 2024 8:41 AM PT
Subject: Nadia Singh finalist packet + proposed final loop

Morgan / Devon / Sarah —

Per the search calibration, sending the finalist packet for Nadia Singh inline below. She is the strongest fit we have seen for the actual brief: taking messy design-partner and early enterprise-adoption learning and turning it into a repeatable customer-growth motion, without treating roadmap exceptions as the job.

This is not a generic enterprise-sales VP readout. I’ve kept the interview notes in the same comparison frame we agreed to use for early calls, then pulled out reference themes and the proposed final topics that seem most worth probing.

-----------------------------------
CANDIDATE SNAPSHOT
-----------------------------------
Name: Nadia Singh
Current lane: customer-growth / enterprise-adoption leadership at growth-stage infrastructure/product companies
Relevant pattern match:
- has built post-design-partner onboarding and expansion motions before there was a mature sales org
- is comfortable with technical buyers, implementation friction, and early product gaps
- repeatedly frames customer trust as “clear boundaries + good follow-through,” not promise-making
- strongest when the company has signal but not yet a system

Why she rose to the top of the slate:
- Other strong candidates tended to drift into classic enterprise-sales language quickly (territory coverage, comp plans, pipeline mechanics, “what can product commit by quarter-end”). Nadia stayed anchored on activation evidence, adoption risk, expansion blockers, and operating handoffs.
- She appears genuinely comfortable in the in-between stage Scaffold is actually in: enough pull to matter, not enough structure to hide behind.

-----------------------------------
INTERVIEW NOTES
-----------------------------------

1) HR calibration screen
Date: Mar 11
Format: 45 min

Repeatable enterprise adoption
- Strongest section of the call.
- Nadia described her best work as turning “founder memory and scattered customer anecdotes” into a small set of repeatable stages, owner handoffs, and leading indicators.
- She asked early what design-partner learning currently lives in people’s heads vs. docs vs. product telemetry.
- She did not assume a big CS function, implementation team, or formal sales engineering layer already exists.

Judgment about not promising product
- Good boundary instinct.
- Said directly that early customer-growth leaders can do real damage if they confuse “earning trust” with “manufacturing certainty.”
- Her framing: if a feature is not committed internally, the external language has to stay at the level of current constraint, current workaround, and what evidence would change prioritization.
- She differentiated packaging/clarity work from true roadmap commitments without being evasive.

Ability to work without a mature sales org
- Comfortable with ambiguity and founder-heavy environments.
- She expects to draft playbooks herself at the beginning.
- Explicitly said she does not need a full RevOps stack to start; wants a reliable source of customer notes, activation milestones, and clear owner routing.
- Watchout: she has usually had at least one operations or program partner by the time the motion starts scaling.

Technical-buyer comfort
- High.
- Spoke fluently about technical evaluators, security/procurement drag, admin setup confusion, and where implementation friction masks as “customer hesitancy.”
- Did not oversell herself as a product manager, but seems able to hold her own with product and engineering leads.

Stage fit
- Good fit for the role as currently calibrated.
- She understands the difference between helping the company learn from enterprise-like customers and prematurely pretending the company is already a fully tooled enterprise vendor.
- Motivated by building the operating system, not inheriting one.

Notes / flags
- Compensation expectations are leadership-level but within the band HR set for the search.
- No odd process concerns from this call.

2) Devon Hayes conversation
Date: Mar 14
Format: 50 min

Repeatable enterprise adoption
- Devon’s note was that she quickly moved from “who are the target accounts?” to “where exactly are people getting stuck between initial excitement and durable usage?”
- She asked how Mercury learning is currently segmented: activation issues, admin/security blockers, procurement friction, expansion stall-outs, and true product deficiency.
- Good instinct to separate noise from pattern before building a motion around it.

Judgment about not promising product
- Strong here as well.
- She said one version of a bad early GTM hire is someone who papers over product gaps with confidence and leaves the company holding informal commitments six weeks later.
- When Devon pushed on enterprise-readiness asks, she did not default to “we’d sell around it.” She asked which items are framing/package issues vs. actual product gaps vs. customer-specific asks that should stay out of scope.
- She did not ask for permission to make bespoke concessions.

Ability to work without a mature sales org
- She seems realistic about working founder-close.
- Comfortable owning the first version of segmentation, account-learning loops, and early expansion criteria.
- She did say that if everything customer-facing still depends on Morgan or Devon translating context live, she would want that made explicit in the first 60 days so she can reduce the dependence rather than fight it.

Technical-buyer comfort
- Devon’s note: “credible with technical buyers without pretending to be eng.”
- She talked about adoption blockers in terms of admin setup, trust, implementation time, and internal champions losing air cover — not just top-of-funnel or quota language.

Stage fit
- Strong.
- Reads as someone who wants to build repeatability from real customer evidence.
- Not a “bring a 20-person field motion on day one” candidate.

Open questions Devon flagged
- How quickly does she prioritize when the backlog has both packaging fixes and real product gaps in it?
- How does she decide what customer-growth owns vs. what stays with founder/product/commercial owners?

3) Sarah Kim conversation
Date: Mar 18
Format: 45 min

Repeatable enterprise adoption
- Sarah came away positive on Nadia’s ability to learn from live customer threads without getting trapped in one-off account servicing.
- Nadia asked what currently happens after customer feedback lands: who synthesizes it, how often, and whether account notes become internal action or just institutional folklore.
- She was especially interested in the handoff from “customer says this matters” to “team can classify this as messaging/package/workaround/product gap.”

Judgment about not promising product
- Sarah pushed directly on this and got a good answer.
- Nadia said she would rather lose speed in the moment than create a trust problem by implying certainty around shipping dates, security posture, or account-specific exceptions.
- She distinguished between giving a customer a credible path and giving them a promise the company cannot support.
- Important: she did not treat customer empathy and firm boundaries as opposites.

Ability to work without a mature sales org
- Comfortable.
- Sarah’s read was that Nadia expects some chaos and is not allergic to doing direct customer work herself.
- She also said that if the role turns into “founder cleanup plus reactive deal support,” it stops being customer-growth and becomes patchwork; that is probably a useful honesty signal.

Technical-buyer comfort
- Strong with customer-facing enterprise-readiness issues.
- Understood the difference between buyer concerns that can be addressed with clearer framing/materials vs. gaps that need product truth behind them.

Stage fit
- Sarah’s note: “best match so far for someone who can inherit the customer thread without turning it into custom promise management.”

Open questions Sarah flagged
- How would Nadia structure the first operating cadence with Sarah on live accounts?
- When does she pull Devon into commercial/procurement framing vs. handling a conversation herself?

4) Recruiter follow-up / close-interest check
Date: Mar 20
Format: 20 min

- Interest level remains high.
- Nadia asked thoughtful questions about how much of the role is expected to be externally visible vs. internally systems-building in the first 90 days.
- She specifically asked whether Scaffold wants a person to “close over rough edges” or a person to make the rough edges legible so the company can build something repeatable. That is directionally aligned with the brief.
- She did not press for title inflation or ask for a sales-heavy org chart underneath her.

-----------------------------------
REFERENCE THEMES
-----------------------------------

Reference 1 — former founder / GM
- Theme: trustworthy translator between customer signal and company action.
- Said Nadia is strongest when the company has a handful of important accounts and lots of ambiguous evidence.
- Credited her with building enough structure that product, founders, and customer-facing people stopped arguing from memory.
- Watchout: can go deeper than some operators expect before declaring a motion “repeatable,” because she is careful about false patterns.

Reference 2 — former product counterpart
- Theme: unusually good judgment on where customer pain should become product work vs. where it needs better framing, onboarding, or owner clarity.
- Said she does not casually promise roadmap items to get through a call.
- Described her as “calm under customer pressure, but not passive.”
- Watchout: wants reciprocal clarity from product/commercial owners; frustration rises if everyone wants her to absorb ambiguity they will not name.

Reference 3 — former implementation / customer-success peer
- Theme: strong operator with technical-buyer credibility.
- Said she is very good at diagnosing whether an expansion stall is really value realization, admin friction, security concern, procurement packaging, or champion weakness.
- Positive note on cross-functional follow-through: if Nadia says she will synthesize patterns and bring back a recommendation, she does.
- Watchout: not the right archetype if the company secretly wants a pure hard-close enterprise seller and is just calling it customer growth.

Cross-reference consistency
- References were notably consistent on three points:
  1) she builds systems out of messy customer evidence,
  2) she is disciplined about not overcommitting product,
  3) she can work across product/commercial/customer lines without blurring ownership.

No material concerns surfaced in references to date.

-----------------------------------
SUMMARY STRENGTHS
-----------------------------------
- Best match to the actual search calibration, especially the “repeatable customer-growth motion from design-partner learning” piece.
- Strong boundary judgment around product promises.
- Credible with technical buyers and enterprise-readiness conversations.
- Comfortable operating before a formal sales/customer org is fully built.
- Thoughtful about owner handoffs instead of assuming everything belongs to the new leader.

-----------------------------------
OPEN PROBES FOR FINAL LOOP
-----------------------------------
1) Prioritization under mixed evidence
She has the pattern recognition, but I would still test how she prioritizes when the input stack includes activation confusion, admin/security asks, procurement friction, and expansion softness all at once.

2) First-90-day operating shape
She clearly knows what “good” looks like; we should probe how lightweight or heavy her first system would be inside a team that is still founder-led in several important places.

3) Handoff discipline with Sarah + Devon
This looks promising, but we should make the boundaries concrete in the final loop so the role is built correctly from the start.

4) Stage stretch vs. support expectations
She is comfortable in a messy environment, but likely most effective if there is at least clarity on source inputs, decision owners, and what not to promise. Worth testing how she behaves if those are incomplete on day one.

-----------------------------------
PROPOSED FINAL INTERVIEW TOPICS
-----------------------------------

I would recommend keeping the final loop tightly scenario-based and explicitly anchored to Mercury/customer-growth realities, not general GTM philosophy.

A) Mercury activation -> repeatable motion
Suggested interviewers: Morgan Chen + Devon Hayes
Goal: test whether Nadia can turn current Mercury activation learning into an operating system without inventing structure we do not have yet.

Prompt area:
- Assume the company has meaningful design-partner signal and a small set of enterprise-leaning accounts, but activation evidence is uneven, founder/customer context is spread across people, and the team needs a repeatable motion more than a top-of-funnel machine.
- Ask Nadia how she would spend the first 30/60/90 days converting that into a working customer-growth rhythm.

What to listen for:
- asks for the minimum viable evidence set rather than a fantasy dashboard
- distinguishes activation friction from broader expansion or commercial issues
- defines a cadence for synthesis and owner routing
- does not reach immediately for headcount/process theater

B) Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals without bespoke promises
Suggested interviewers: Devon Hayes + Sarah Kim
Goal: probe how she handles real enterprise pressure while staying within current product truth.

Prompt area:
- Present the current shape of enterprise-readiness pressure in a bounded way: SSO timing questions, admin-change audit history, clearer admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and requests for a standalone procurement packet.
- Make clear that commercial/procurement framing has an owner, customer-thread continuity has an owner, and dates/quotes/feature promises are not available before those features ship.
- Ask Nadia how she would help the company learn from those signals and communicate credibly without turning each conversation into custom roadmap negotiation.

What to listen for:
- separates packaging/framing work from product commitments
- knows when to pull Devon vs. Sarah vs. product facts
- can preserve customer trust without inventing dates or exceptions
- does not drift into “we can probably make that work” language

C) Expansion failure modes and leading indicators
Suggested interviewer: Morgan Chen
Goal: understand how Nadia thinks about the point after activation when accounts stall, wobble, or fail to broaden.

Prompt area:
- Ask what failure modes she would expect to see early in Mercury-like accounts: weak championing, admin friction, unclear value realization, setup trust issues, procurement drag, poor handoff after initial enthusiasm, etc.
- Ask which of those she would instrument first, which require direct customer work vs. internal process fixes, and how she would tell the difference between a product problem and a motion problem.

What to listen for:
- practical diagnosis framework
- evidence-first approach
- comfort with incomplete instrumentation
- disciplined ownership mapping rather than “customer-growth owns everything customer-ish”

D) Handoffs with Sarah Kim and Devon Hayes
Suggested interviewers: Sarah Kim + Morgan Chen
Goal: make sure the role plugs into the existing owner split cleanly.

Prompt area:
- Ask Nadia to sketch how she would work with Sarah on live customer threads and with Devon on commercial/procurement framing.
- Include an example where a customer request sits partly in packaging, partly in product gap, and partly in account education.

What to listen for:
- explicit owner boundaries
- respect for existing customer thread continuity
- willingness to systematize instead of bypassing current owners
- no assumption that taking over externally means absorbing every internal decision

E) Stage fit / first build
Suggested interviewer: HR or Morgan Chen, depending on schedule
Goal: confirm she is opting into this stage with clear eyes.

Prompt area:
- Ask what support she would need to be effective here, what she would build herself, and what signals would tell her the motion is becoming repeatable.
- Ask what she would not try to build in quarter one.

What to listen for:
- realism about stage constraints
- ability to choose sequence over completeness
- appetite for building from signal, not from organizational prestige

-----------------------------------
TOPICS I WOULD AVOID IN THE FINAL LOOP
-----------------------------------
- Hypothetical feature-date negotiation.
- “How would you close this one enterprise logo no matter what?” prompts.
- Open-ended territory/pipeline scaling questions that imply we are hiring a conventional VP Sales.

Morgan Chen · Scaffold
Purpose: durable record of what this search was scoped to do and what it explicitly did not authorize. Read this before reusing the role as justification for any current GTM, staffing, or roadmap language.

ORIGIN AND DECISION CHAIN
- Decision opened Feb 26-27, 2024 in the post-Series B leadership reset. Internal line was "more room, same discipline — a defensible story, not a bigger one." The Series B close was not permission to describe Mercury as enterprise-ready or to reopen every deferred initiative.
- It was the first new leadership search to scope after the reset. The second Mercury engineering req was explicitly not reopened and stayed closed.
- Devon Hayes + HR drafted the first role description. Morgan Chen reviewed before anything went wider than the small reset group.
- Apr 15, 2024: Nadia Singh started as Head of Customer Growth, reporting to Morgan. This was the planned leader, not a raise-driven acceleration.
- Jun 18, 2024 read with Devon: input quality still manual; cadence useful but not yet clean enough to justify another GTM layer. No RevOps, CS, SDR, or field-sales lane opened in Q3.
- Jun 20, 2025: Nadia's final day. Wind-down-not-backfill was the ruling. No Head of Customer Growth replacement search. Next hire is role-fit only and revisits after the customer-growth alpha.

WHAT THE SEARCH WAS MEANT TO ACHIEVE
- Build a repeatable customer-growth motion out of Mercury / Evergreen-like pull — turn founder memory and scattered customer anecdotes into a small set of repeatable stages, owner handoffs, and leading indicators.
- Help the company learn from enterprise-leaning accounts without prematurely pretending Scaffold is a fully tooled enterprise vendor.
- Earn customer trust through clear boundaries and good follow-through, not promise-making. External language stays at the level of current constraint, current workaround, and what evidence would change prioritization.
- Capture patterns across five recurring shapes: activation friction, admin handoff / role confusion, procurement and security packaging, expansion stalls after first live sync, and true product gaps.
- First-90-day scope: pattern capture and repeatability around Mercury activation, Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals, and expansion failure modes.
- Operate without a mature sales org — draft the first playbooks herself, define a reliable source of customer notes, activation milestones, and clear owner routing.
- Build enough structure that product, founders, and customer-facing people stop arguing from memory.

WHAT THE SEARCH DID NOT AUTHORIZE
- A new GTM, Customer Success, RevOps, SDR, or field-sales org layer. No such lane was opened during the role, and none was authorized as a follow-on.
- Series C narrative, raise-driven headcount acceleration, or "we hired the planned leader" being conflated with "we are accelerating because we raised." Hired-the-planned-leader and accelerating-because-we-raised are not the same thing.
- Bespoke commitments or product-roadmap negotiating per account. Customer empathy and firm boundaries are not opposites; one version of a bad early GTM hire is someone who papers over product gaps with confidence and leaves the company holding informal commitments six weeks later.
- Product facts or roadmap authority. The leader's prior involvement does not transfer to product truth or roadmap authorization.
- Lighthouse-logo thinking as the primary customer-growth outcome.
- Org-chart-heavy first-90-day language, headcount theater, or a fantasy dashboard before a minimum viable evidence set exists.
- Backfill after Nadia's exit. customer_growth_v1 = wind-down-not-backfill. Any next hire is role-fit only and revisits post customer-growth alpha.
- Reopening the second Mercury engineering req. That decision stayed closed; if Mercury engineering hiring reopens later, the evidence rule still stands: senior for repeated platform / architecture seam failures needing independent ownership; implementation-heavy mid-level for hardening / throughput constraints; no req if the current split closes the remaining work.
- Promises — explicit or implied — about SSO timing, admin-change audit history, admin-vs-billing-owner separation, or a procurement packet shipping on any timeline.
- Treating Mercury as enterprise-ready or reopening every deferred initiative. Evergreen Bank stays a useful stress case for the current path, not a reason to convert wave-1 learning into bespoke-build behavior.

OWNER-LANE MAP THAT HELD UNDER THIS ROLE
- Jake — Mercury execution and the weekly launch-evidence path; MER-1279 as the internal operating ledger.
- Leo Park — platform seams and release discipline.
- Priya — activation / onboarding UX, admin / setup clarity, failure-state legibility.
- Anna Martinez — retention evidence, cohort-definition discipline, board-consistent outside-reader package.
- Devon Hayes + Sarah Kim — enterprise-readiness commercial framing and procurement packaging; Sarah holds the customer / external coordination thread.
- Morgan Chen — board follow-through, sequencing, dates / promises / not-yet lines, hiring sequence.
- Customer-growth leader reported to Morgan and did not absorb those lanes.

DURABLE RULES FOR REUSING THIS ARCHIVE
- Do not cite the 2024 search as justification for opening a GTM/CS/RevOps/SDR/field-sales lane. No such lane was authorized by this search.
- Do not cite it as Series C, fundraising, or repeatable-growth proof. Evergreen = annual-account win + current-state enterprise-readiness evidence, not repeatable growth proof by itself.
- Do not transfer Nadia's prior Compass involvement into product facts, roadmap authority, or behavior-change evidence.
- Do not describe Mercury as enterprise-ready because this role existed.
- If a future customer-growth hire is proposed, frame it as role-fit only against the customer-growth alpha, and keep the Q2 freeze-style rule until evidence clears another cadence.

Date written: 2026-09-14
Owner lane: Procurement / security reviewer (Evergreen)
Subject: Evergreen's January 2024 current-flow examples pack — circulate status and whether it constituted a complete procurement/security packet

1. Was the pack cleared to circulate?
- Cleared for internal routing by Evergreen's procurement and security reviewers on 2024-01-05. Their reasoning: the concrete-example format was specific enough to circulate without sliding into a roadmap conversation.
- The pack was part of a small, bounded "circulate-now" set, alongside the bounded-flow summary and the written current-state answers (the latter explicitly separating current Mercury behavior from later enterprise-readiness evaluation).
- Not cleared as a roadmap artifact, a roadmap-SLA artifact, or as a substitute for written procurement/security Q&A. Reviewers accepted it on the basis of specificity about the current product, not as a promise about future behavior.

2. Was it a complete procurement/security packet?
- No — it was a usable subset, not a complete packet.
- It covered current-flow specifics: first admin, second admin, delayed or failed first live sync, invite or resend, source connection or disconnection, and the audit-history caveat. As of 2024-01-09 it had expanded to also cover inviting or resending an invite, changing role type, and connecting or disconnecting a source.
- Real-source connection in the current product flow was validated by Evergreen, which is what made the pack suitable for routing.
- What it did not contain: explicit procurement/security Q&A, termination-handling terms, deletion-process commitments, tenant SLA commitments, certification evidence, or connector-deletion-procedure language. Those were settled separately (counsel accepted termination-handling and existing platform deletion-process on the contract redline, 2024-08-05 closed 2024-09-08; 24h tenant-SLA, certification, and connector-deletion-procedure were dropped).
- The pack was also explicitly kept separate from overage-smoothing / commercial terms, which Evergreen treats as standard Growth with no exception.

3. Bottom line for the archive
- Cleared to circulate: yes, internally, as bounded current-state evidence.
- Complete procurement/security packet: no. It was the examples layer of a larger circulating set and was never intended to stand alone for legal/security sign-off. Procurement/security review relied on it for specificity; contractual commitments lived in the redline, not in the examples pack.

tests.request: Create a historical Honeycomb alert-handling note for December 23, 2023 through January 1, 2024, covering thresholds, paging, escalation, and quiet-week reporting.

input.query: Honeycomb alert handling escalation on-call 2023
quiet week holiday incident response procedure

input.body:
Scope: Scaffold production API + sync workers. Window: Sat 2023-12-23 00:00 PT through Mon 2024-01-01 23:59 PT. Written retroactively from the standing operating posture in effect during that window and the alert-routing decisions made with Leo on the API v2 contract work.

Thresholds (Honeycomb triggers active over the window)
  - API v2 p95 latency > 800 ms for 5 min — warning, no page.
  - API v2 error rate > 1.0% of requests for 5 min — warning, no page.
  - Sync worker queue depth > 10k for 10 min — warning, no page.
  - Connector heartbeat missed for > 15 min on any tenant — warning, no page.
  - API v2 p95 latency > 1500 ms for 5 min OR error rate > 3.0% for 3 min — page.
  - Sync worker queue depth > 50k for 10 min OR worker pool > 90% saturated for 10 min — page.
  - Auth (JWT) 5xx > 0.5% for 3 min — page (skew-window aware; 10-min clock-skew tolerance documented, 5-min verification leeway in JWT docs PR).
  - Webhook delivery failure > 5% sustained 10 min — page.

Paging
  - Primary: on-call rotation (Leo primary for API/auth, Jake primary for sync/connector heartbeat over the holiday window per his "workspace is live" ownership).
  - Secondary: Morgan as backup for any page that does not ack within 10 min.
  - Channel: PagerDuty → SMS first, then phone tree. No Slack-only paging; Slack is FYI only.
  - Quiet-hours behavior unchanged across the window: pages fire as written, ack-SLA still 10 min. No "holiday silence" mode.

Escalation
  - L1 (on-call): ack in 10 min, mitigate within 30 min, post a 1-line status in #incidents within 30 min of mitigation start.
  - L2 (Leo / Jake depending on lane): engaged if mitigation not in flight by 30 min OR if a second paging trigger fires within 60 min of the first.
  - L3 (Morgan): engaged if L2 cannot establish a mitigation path within 60 min, OR for any auth/JWT incident regardless of L2 status, OR for any tenant-impacting data-loss signal.
  - Customer-facing comms held at L3 only; copy stays narrow (operating hygiene, no roadmap or staffing language).

Quiet-week reporting (2023-12-23 → 2024-01-01)
  - Window is treated as one continuous quiet week. No cadence changes to thresholds or paging.
  - Daily 09:00 PT summary in #eng-oncall: triggers fired, pages fired, MTTA, MTTR, open follow-ups. Single message, highlights-only.
  - Owner status update cadence: one consolidated Monday-morning note (Mon 2023-12-25 was Christmas — skipped; Mon 2024-01-01 was New Year's Day — skipped). Mid-week note on Wed 2023-12-27. Both kept to the 4-section format (team / customers / investors-board / legal-ops), 3–4 bullets per section.
  - Postmortems: any page that fires produces a one-page postmortem within 5 business days of the window closing; owner-only review, no broad distribution during the quiet week.
  - Customer comms: proactive only for incidents matching the page criteria above; no scheduled customer emails, no roadmap/status outreach during the window.

Notes carried forward
  - "Workspace is live" stays Jake's lane for the holiday window — no expansion to other owners.
  - Webhook/JWT routing follows the v2 contract examples Leo owns; do not invent a new route during the window.
  - Owner messages in this window follow the deliberate-state rule, not reactive Monday AM cadence.

# Mercury Planning — May 2023 Archive
Archived: 2026-09-14

## Operating work (coordinated here)
Mercury served as the team's operating spine throughout May 2023. Operating coordination was carried in protected working blocks (e.g., the May 8, 2023 calendar block) and continued through planning work mid-month (as of 2023-05-10) and internal follow-ups after the May 19 NYC visit. The intent for that follow-up was explicit: keep the work internal and operating-focused rather than letting it migrate into deck material.

## Investor-deck work (prioritization)
The investor deck was deliberately deferred during this period. As of 2023-05-26, the deck was held back until two conditions were tighter: launch inputs and Mercury proof points. Sequence: launch first, deck second. No deck work was being driven from Mercury operating findings until those proof points were cleaner.

## How the two were kept separate
- Mercury work lived in protected calendar blocks and internal channels, not in deck drafting.
- NYC visit follow-up (5/19) was scoped as operating/internal — not framed as investor material.
- Deck deferral was conditional, not indefinite: gated on launch inputs + proof points, both tracked as of 5/26.

## Open at end of May
- Launch inputs: still being tightened.
- Mercury proof points: not yet clean enough to support deck work.
- Deck: still deferred; no carry-over commitment beyond the gating conditions above.

- A copy-only preview clarification to Mercury v0.2 — not a change to activation, bands, or surface. Preview stays separate from activation.

- Conditional on current release-readiness reviewers confirming it adds no risk.
- Specifically (Leo Park): must fit existing frames and preserve existing event names; otherwise wait.

Announcement:
- The v0.2 clarification was posted to Discord #eng-releases, not #eng-all. If the PR cites the announcement channel, that is the channel.

1. Replace any "approved" / "cleared" wording with "reviewer-approved, pending release-readiness sign-off".
2. Remove any implication that the clarification altered activation, bands, or the Evergreen budget posture.
3. State Leo's fit-and-event-names condition explicitly where the release condition is described.

## The five categories

1. **Activation friction**
   - Definition: workspace stalls before activation, or around it. Activated = `real_source_connected` OR `first_live_sync_completed` within 7 days.
   - Evidence sources: Anna metrics cut, Jake support examples, setup notes.
   - Example pattern: `admin_first_action` without `first_live_sync_completed` inside day 7; setup looks active before real value lands.

2. **Admin handoff and role confusion**
   - Definition: interpretation problems around roles, authority, resend/remove actions, source-workspace wording, and visible admin state.
   - Evidence sources: Sarah continuity notes, Jake support examples.
   - Example pattern: role label over-read when resend/remove powers aren't visible on the same surface; stale visible admin state after cancel.

3. **Procurement / security packaging**
   - Definition: current product truth getting translated into buyer / security / procurement requirements faster than the product can safely generalize.
   - Evidence sources: Sarah continuity notes, Devon caveat page.
   - Example pattern: audit wording implying export/reporting; SSO timing ask; admin vs billing language.

4. **Expansion stalls after first live sync**
   - Definition: `first_live_sync_completed` happens, but follow-through doesn't broaden into broader use.
   - Evidence sources: Anna metrics cut, support notes, customer thread notes.
   - Example pattern: first live sync lands but no second admin motion; champion enthusiasm outruns implementation confidence.

5. **True product gaps**
   - Definition: a repeated issue that survives wording / support / packaging fixes and needs a product-owner lane.
   - Evidence sources: repeated internal examples, product review input.
   - Example pattern: durable capability gap after copy/support fixes; workflow gap with no stable workaround.

## The ownership rule

Every row carries an owner route. Customer-growth is NOT a holding pen — every uncomfortable customer issue must have a next live owner attached, or it stays a sighting, not a finding.

- Activation friction → Jake (support lane); Anna owns the metrics anchor.

- She also said that if the role turns into “founder cleanup plus reactive deal support,” it stops being customer-growth and becomes patchwork; that is probably a useful honesty signal.

Technical-buyer comfort
- Strong with customer-facing enterprise-readiness issues.
- Understood the difference between buyer concerns that can be addressed with clearer framing/materials vs. gaps that need product truth behind them.

Stage fit
- Sarah’s note: “best match so far for someone who can inherit the customer thread without turning it into custom promise management.”

Open questions Sarah flagged
- How would Nadia structure the first operating cadence with Sarah on live accounts?
- When does she pull Devon into commercial/procurement framing vs. handling a conversation herself?

4) Recruiter follow-up / close-interest check
Date: Mar 20
Format: 20 min

- Interest level remains high.
- Nadia asked thoughtful questions about how much of the role is expected to be externally visible vs. internally systems-building in the first 90 days.
- She specifically asked whether Scaffold wants a person to “close over rough edges” or a person to make the rough edges legible so the company can build something repeatable. That is directionally aligned with the brief.
- She did not press for title inflation or ask for a sales-heavy org chart underneath her.

-----------------------------------
REFERENCE THEMES
-----------------------------------

Reference 1 — former founder / GM
- Theme: trustworthy translator between customer signal and company action.
- Said Nadia is strongest when the company has a handful of important accounts and lots of ambiguous evidence.
- Credited her with building enough structure that product, founders, and customer-facing people stopped arguing from memory.
- Watchout: can go deeper than some operators expect before declaring a motion “repeatable,” because she is careful about false patterns.

Reference 2 — former product counterpart
- Theme: unusually good judgment on where customer pain should become product work vs. where it needs better framing, onboarding, or owner clarity.
- Said she does not casually promise roadmap items to get through a call.
- Described her as “calm under customer pressure, but not passive.”
- Watchout: wants reciprocal clarity from product/commercial owners; frustration rises if everyone wants her to absorb ambiguity they will not name.

Reference 3 — former implementation / customer-success peer
- Theme: strong operator with technical-buyer credibility.
- Said she is very good at diagnosing whether an expansion stall is really value realization, admin friction, security concern, procurement packaging, or champion weakness.
- Positive note on cross-functional follow-through: if Nadia says she will synthesize patterns and bring back a recommendation, she does.
- Watchout: not the right archetype if the company secretly wants a pure hard-close enterprise seller and is just calling it customer growth.

Cross-reference consistency
- References were notably consistent on three points:
  1) she builds systems out of messy customer evidence,
  2) she is disciplined about not overcommitting product,
  3) she can work across product/commercial/customer lines without blurring ownership.

No material concerns surfaced in references to date.

-----------------------------------
SUMMARY STRENGTHS
-----------------------------------
- Best match to the actual search calibration, especially the “repeatable customer-growth motion from design-partner learning” piece.
- Strong boundary judgment around product promises.
- Credible with technical buyers and enterprise-readiness conversations.
- Comfortable operating before a formal sales/customer org is fully built.
- Thoughtful about owner handoffs instead of assuming everything belongs to the new leader.

-----------------------------------
OPEN PROBES FOR FINAL LOOP
-----------------------------------
1) Prioritization under mixed evidence
She has the pattern recognition, but I would still test how she prioritizes when the input stack includes activation confusion, admin/security asks, procurement friction, and expansion softness all at once.

2) First-90-day operating shape
She clearly knows what “good” looks like; we should probe how lightweight or heavy her first system would be inside a team that is still founder-led in several important places.

3) Handoff discipline with Sarah + Devon
This looks promising, but we should make the boundaries concrete in the final loop so the role is built correctly from the start.

4) Stage stretch vs. support expectations
She is comfortable in a messy environment, but likely most effective if there is at least clarity on source inputs, decision owners, and what not to promise. Worth testing how she behaves if those are incomplete on day one.

-----------------------------------
PROPOSED FINAL INTERVIEW TOPICS
-----------------------------------

I would recommend keeping the final loop tightly scenario-based and explicitly anchored to Mercury/customer-growth realities, not general GTM philosophy.

A) Mercury activation -> repeatable motion
Suggested interviewers: Morgan Chen + Devon Hayes
Goal: test whether Nadia can turn current Mercury activation learning into an operating system without inventing structure we do not have yet.

Prompt area:
- Assume the company has meaningful design-partner signal and a small set of enterprise-leaning accounts, but activation evidence is uneven, founder/customer context is spread across people, and the team needs a repeatable motion more than a top-of-funnel machine.
- Ask Nadia how she would spend the first 30/60/90 days converting that into a working customer-growth rhythm.

What to listen for:
- asks for the minimum viable evidence set rather than a fantasy dashboard
- distinguishes activation friction from broader expansion or commercial issues
- defines a cadence for synthesis and owner routing
- does not reach immediately for headcount/process theater

B) Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals without bespoke promises
Suggested interviewers: Devon Hayes + Sarah Kim
Goal: probe how she handles real enterprise pressure while staying within current product truth.

Prompt area:
- Present the current shape of enterprise-readiness pressure in a bounded way: SSO timing questions, admin-change audit history, clearer admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and requests for a standalone procurement packet.
- Make clear that commercial/procurement framing has an owner, customer-thread continuity has an owner, and dates/quotes/feature promises are not available before those features ship.
- Ask Nadia how she would help the company learn from those signals and communicate credibly without turning each conversation into custom roadmap negotiation.

What to listen for:
- separates packaging/framing work from product commitments
- knows when to pull Devon vs. Sarah vs. product facts
- can preserve customer trust without inventing dates or exceptions
- does not drift into “we can probably make that work” language

C) Expansion failure modes and leading indicators
Suggested interviewer: Morgan Chen
Goal: understand how Nadia thinks about the point after activation when accounts stall, wobble, or fail to broaden.

Prompt area:
- Ask what failure modes she would expect to see early in Mercury-like accounts: weak championing, admin friction, unclear value realization, setup trust issues, procurement drag, poor handoff after initial enthusiasm, etc.
- Ask which of those she would instrument first, which require direct customer work vs. internal process fixes, and how she would tell the difference between a product problem and a motion problem.

What to listen for:
- practical diagnosis framework
- evidence-first approach
- comfort with incomplete instrumentation
- disciplined ownership mapping rather than “customer-growth owns everything customer-ish”

D) Handoffs with Sarah Kim and Devon Hayes
Suggested interviewers: Sarah Kim + Morgan Chen
Goal: make sure the role plugs into the existing owner split cleanly.

Prompt area:
- Ask Nadia to sketch how she would work with Sarah on live customer threads and with Devon on commercial/procurement framing.
- Include an example where a customer request sits partly in packaging, partly in product gap, and partly in account education.

What to listen for:
- explicit owner boundaries
- respect for existing customer thread continuity
- willingness to systematize instead of bypassing current owners
- no assumption that taking over externally means absorbing every internal decision

E) Stage fit / first build
Suggested interviewer: HR or Morgan Chen, depending on schedule
Goal: confirm she is opting into this stage with clear eyes.

Prompt area:
- Ask what support she would need to be effective here, what she would build herself, and what signals would tell her the motion is becoming repeatable.
- Ask what she would not try to build in quarter one.

What to listen for:
- realism about stage constraints
- ability to choose sequence over completeness
- appetite for building from signal, not from organizational prestige

-----------------------------------
TOPICS I WOULD AVOID IN THE FINAL LOOP
-----------------------------------
- Hypothetical feature-date negotiation.
- “How would you close this one enterprise logo no matter what?” prompts.
- Open-ended territory/pipeline scaling questions that imply we are hiring a conventional VP Sales.
- Any framing that encourages bespoke roadmap promises for Evergreen-like accounts.
- Debates about broader product scope outside the current Mercury/customer-growth boundary.

-----------------------------------
HR RECOMMENDATION ON PROCESS
-----------------------------------
- Keep the final loop to 2-3 tightly run conversations, not a sprawling panel.
- Use one shared scenario spine so answers can be compared across interviewers.
- Finish with a same-day debrief focused on the agreed dimensions above, rather than generic executive-impression language.

If helpful, I can turn the proposed topics into a tighter interviewer guide once you decide who you want in the final loop.

Can you turn the proposed loop into a tight final interview plan? I want it to probe Mercury activation, Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals, expansion failure modes, and handoffs with Sarah and Devon — without inviting bespoke roadmap promises or turning this into a generic VP Sales interview.

FINAL INTERVIEW LOOP — NADIA SINGH (CG-A)

Shape: 3 sessions, ~3 hours total candidate time, one shared scenario spine (a Mercury-like customer at the design-partner -> early-enterprise boundary). Same-day 30-min debrief with an explicit decision rubric. Tight by design — no panel sprawl.

SESSION 1 — Mercury activation + expansion failure modes (75 min)
  Interviewers: Morgan + Devon
  Covers: HR topics A + C
  Scenario 1A (~30 min) — "You join Monday. Founder/customer context lives across Devon, Sarah, Morgan, and scattered notes. Activation evidence is uneven. Walk us through 30/60/90."
    Listen for: minimum viable evidence ask (not a fantasy dashboard); activation friction separated from expansion/commercial noise; synthesis + owner-routing cadence; no immediate headcount/process theater; respect for existing founder-led lanes.
  Scenario 1B (~30 min) — "Six weeks in, two Mercury accounts stall after initial enthusiasm. Diagnose before you instrument."
    Listen for: practical diagnosis framework (weak champion / admin friction / unclear value / setup trust / procurement drag / handoff weakness); evidence-first approach; comfort with incomplete instrumentation; disciplined ownership mapping rather than "customer-growth owns everything customer-ish."
  Buffer / follow-ups (~15 min).

SESSION 2 — Enterprise-readiness under pressure + handoff discipline (75 min)
  Interviewers: Devon + Sarah (Devon leads); Morgan optional
  Covers: HR topics B + D
  Scenario spine — a customer raises (a) SSO timing, (b) admin-change audit history, (c) clearer admin-vs-billing-owner separation, (d) a standalone procurement packet. Make explicit in the prompt:
    - Commercial/procurement framing has an owner (Devon's lane).
    - Customer-thread continuity has an owner (Sarah's lane).
    - Dates/quotes/feature commitments are not available before features ship.
  Probe:
    - How does she help the company learn from these signals without each conversation turning into custom roadmap negotiation?
    - How does she work with Sarah on the live thread and Devon on commercial framing?
    - In a request that splits across packaging + product gap + account education, where does she sit and where do Sarah/Devon sit?
  Listen for: separation of packaging/framing work from product commitments; owner-routing instinct (Devon vs Sarah vs product facts); customer trust preserved without inventing dates or exceptions; no "we can probably make that work" drift.

SESSION 3 — Stage fit / first build (45 min)
  Interviewer: Morgan (solo) or HR-led with Morgan present
  Covers: HR topic E
  Prompts:
    - What would you build yourself in Q1?
    - What would you NOT try to build in Q1?
    - What support do you need to be effective here?
    - What signals tell you the motion is becoming repeatable?
  Listen for: realism about stage constraints; sequence over completeness; appetite for building from signal, not from org-chart prestige; comfort with founder-led lanes that won't go away immediately.

DEBRIEF — same day, 30 min
  Attendees: Morgan + Devon + Sarah + HR
  Decision rubric — anchored to your four probes plus one meta-dimension:
    1. Mercury activation — design-partner signal -> working rhythm without process theater?
    2. Enterprise-readiness without bespoke promises — framing work vs. product truth under real pressure?
    3. Expansion failure modes — diagnosis before instrumentation, with ownership discipline?
    4. Handoffs with Sarah + Devon — clean owner split, no bypass of existing threads?
    5. (Meta) Stage fit / first-build realism.
  Decision: proceed to offer / hold for second pass / pass. No generic executive-impression language.

AVOID-LIST — lock these in for the final loop
  - Hypothetical feature-date negotiation prompts.
  - "Close this one enterprise logo no matter what" framings.
  - Open-ended territory/pipeline scaling questions implying a conventional VP Sales hire.
  - Anything that invites bespoke roadmap promises for Evergreen-style accounts.
  - Debates about broader product scope outside the current Mercury/customer-growth boundary.
  - Lighthouse-logo thinking presented as the primary customer-growth outcome.
  - Org-chart-heavy first-90-day language.
  - Promises — explicit or implied — about SSO timing, audit history, admin-vs-billing-owner separation, or a procurement packet shipping on any timeline.

Sofia

Purpose: raw Q2 operating evidence for Sofia before drafting the board note. These are factual inputs only, not board language.

1) Hiring pace after the Series B — raw evidence

Revisit trigger is external launch-readiness feedback from design-partner conversations/trials, not an arbitrary calendar date. Decision rule still depends on whether blockers look like senior platform/architecture seams, implementation throughput, or manageable current-team follow-through.

Customer-growth leader
- Apr 15 Nadia Singh started as Head of Customer Growth. Reporting line: Morgan. First-90-day scope: build repeatable customer-growth motion around Mercury activation, Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals, expansion failure modes, and handoffs with Sarah Kim and Devon Hayes.

2) Atlas risk after Rishi’s departure — raw evidence

Current lane: customer-growth / enterprise-adoption leadership at growth-stage infrastructure/product companies
Relevant pattern match:
- has built post-design-partner onboarding and expansion motions before there was a mature sales org
- is comfortable with technical buyers, implementation friction, and early product gaps
- repeatedly frames customer trust as “clear boundaries + good follow-through,” not promise-making
- strongest when the company has signal but not yet a system

- Other strong candidates tended to drift into classic enterprise-sales language quickly (territory coverage, comp plans, pipeline mechanics, “what can product commit by quarter-end”). Nadia stayed anchored on activation evidence, adoption risk, expansion blockers, and operating handoffs.

-----------------------------------

1) HR calibration screen
Date: Mar 11
Format: 45 min

Repeatable enterprise adoption
- Strongest section of the call.
- Nadia described her best work as turning “founder memory and scattered customer anecdotes” into a small set of repeatable stages, owner handoffs, and leading indicators.
- She asked early what design-partner learning currently lives in people’s heads vs. docs vs. product telemetry.
- She did not assume a big CS function, implementation team, or formal sales engineering layer already exists.

Judgment about not promising product
- Good boundary instinct.
- Said directly that early customer-growth leaders can do real damage if they confuse “earning trust” with “manufacturing certainty.”
- Her framing: if a feature is not committed internally, the external language has to stay at the level of current constraint, current workaround, and what evidence would change prioritization.
- She differentiated packaging/clarity work from true roadmap commitments without being evasive.

Ability to work without a mature sales org
- Comfortable with ambiguity and founder-heavy environments.
- She expects to draft playbooks herself at the beginning.
- Explicitly said she does not need a full RevOps stack to start; wants a reliable source of customer notes, activation milestones, and clear owner routing.
- Watchout: she has usually had at least one operations or program partner by the time the motion starts scaling.

Technical-buyer comfort
- High.
- Spoke fluently about technical evaluators, security/procurement drag, admin setup confusion, and where implementation friction masks as “customer hesitancy.”
- Did not oversell herself as a product manager, but seems able to hold her own with product and engineering leads.

Stage fit
- Good fit for the role as currently calibrated.
- She understands the difference between helping the company learn from enterprise-like customers and prematurely pretending the company is already a fully tooled enterprise vendor.
- Motivated by building the operating system, not inhe…

  Covers: HR topics A + C

  Decision: proceed to offer / hold for second pass / pass. No generic executive-impression language.

  - Hypothetical feature-date negotiation prompts.
  - "Close this one enterprise logo no matter what" framings.
  - Open-ended territory/pipeline scaling questions implying a conventional VP Sales hire.
  - Anything that invites bespoke roadmap promises for…

- If we believe our own reset, CG-A.
- I am fine moving CG-A into final references, but I would keep the offer gate closed until those calls are done and we have one more Morgan + Devon calibration pass.

DECISION MEMO — customer-growth search (pre-offer)
Date: 2024-03-21
Authors: Morgan Chen (with Devon's compare as the source record)
Status: deliberation. Offer gate held. Not for circulation beyond Morgan + Devon until references + calibration pass are complete.

THE BRIEF AS RESET (the actual job to be done)
- Turn Mercury / Evergreen-style learning into a repeatable adoption and expansion motion — not a sequence of bespoke design-partner wins.
- Stay off the roadmap-as-promise habit. Hard boundary between shipped, packaging, and later.
- Operate alongside founders, with no mature SDR / AE / SE / RevOps layer underneath.
- Technical-buyer comfort directly. No hiding behind a solutions team.
- Builder for the stage we are in. Not a pipeline / forecast machine for a later stage.

CG-A vs the brief
- Adoption motion: has actually turned messy design-partner learning into a rollout and expansion pattern. Talks milestones and handoffs, not lighthouse logos. Matches.
- Roadmap discipline: explicit line against selling future state as if shipped. Matches.
- Operating without a mature org: prior examples assume founder-side ambiguity and limited systems. Matches.
- Technical buyers: direct with security, IT, ops, and technical champions. Matches.
- Stage fit: builder for where we are. Matches.
- Gap to flag in references: less classically polished in the VP-Sales mold. We are choosing this anyway because the brief is the brief.

CG-B vs the brief — a fit question, not a strength question
- Adoption motion: strong closer on strategic deals; design partners read as logos, not raw material for a repeatable motion. Does not match.
- Roadmap discipline: answers drifted toward future-state vision + exec alignment to drag the company forward. Does not match. This is the exact habit we reset away from.

EARLY-CALL DEBRIEF TEMPLATE
Customer-Growth / GTM Leader Search (2024)
Reconstructed 2026-09-14 from the comparison frame actually used across early screens, per the HR Mar-22 finalist packet and Devon Hayes' Mar-21 finalist compare (CG-A / CG-B).

PURPOSE
One-page per candidate. Same shape for every early call so two candidates can be compared without re-reading the room. Early calls answer two questions only: does this person fit the reset brief, and is the gap (if any) something later loops can close?

THE BRIEF AS RESET (anchor every row below to this)
- Turn Mercury / Evergreen-style learning into a repeatable adoption and expansion motion — not a sequence of bespoke design-partner wins.
- Hard boundary between shipped, packaging, and later scope. Roadmap is not a promise.
- Operate alongside founders with no mature SDR / AE / SE / RevOps layer underneath.
- Direct with security, IT, ops, and technical champions. No hiding behind a solutions team.
- Builder for the stage we are in. Not a pipeline / forecast machine for a later stage.

CANDIDATE
Name / current lane / referral source / screen date / interviewer / format / length.

WHY THIS CANDIDATE IS IN THE ROOM
Two or three lines. Pattern match to the reset brief. What HR thought they saw.

COMPARISON FRAME — score 1–4 in every row, write one line of evidence per row
(1 = does not match / actively wrong habit; 2 = partial, mostly a stage mismatch; 3 = matches with caveats; 4 = clean match)

1. Repeatable enterprise adoption
   Evidence: Did they talk in milestones, owner handoffs, and what becomes reusable? Or did they treat design partners as lighthouse logos and the motion as a sequence of one-offs?
   Listen for: minimum viable evidence ask; activation friction separated from expansion / commercial noise; synthesis + owner-routing cadence; no immediate headcount / process theater.

2. Judgment about not promising product
   Evidence: Hard boundary between shipped, packaging, and later scope? Or did answers drift toward selling future-state vision and pulling exec alignment to drag the company forward?
   Listen for: separates packaging/clarity work from true roadmap commitments; gives the customer a credible path without inventing dates or exceptions; no "we can probably make that work" drift.

3. Ability to work without a mature sales org
   Evidence: Real examples of founder-side ambiguity, limited systems, no SDR layer? Or did most examples assume AE / SE / RevOps support earlier than we have?
   Listen for: drafts playbooks themselves at the start; wants reliable customer notes, activation milestones, and clear owner routing rather than a stack; willing to do direct customer work herself.

4. Technical-buyer comfort
   Evidence: Direct with security, IT, ops, and technical champions? Or did the deeper technical detail sit with a separate solutions / product counterpart?
   Listen for: fluency on technical evaluators, security / procurement drag, admin setup confusion, and where implementation friction masks as "customer hesitancy"; does not oversell as a PM but holds her own with eng.

5. Stage fit
   Evidence: Builder for the stage we are in, or right person for a later stage we have not reached?
   Listen for: understands the difference between helping the company learn from enterprise-like customers and prematurely pretending the company is already a fully tooled enterprise vendor; appetite for building from signal, not from org-chart prestige.

REFERENCE THEMES (if reference checks have happened)
- Cross-reference consistency on (a) building systems out of messy customer evidence, (b) discipline on not overcommitting product, (c) cross-functional follow-through without blurring ownership.
- Watchouts named consistently across references.

NOTES / FLAGS
- Compensation expectation vs. band.
- Odd process concerns (none, schedule friction, references not yet returned, etc.).
- Watchouts specific to this person (e.g. "has usually had at least one ops / program partner by the time the motion starts scaling" — note the cost of that gap, not just the fact).

DECISION (one of three, no fourth option)
- Advance to finalist loop.
- Hold for second pass / more evidence.
- Pass — with the reason written in one sentence.

DECISION LIMITS — applied before the Decision line is written
- No advance if any single row is a 1. A 1 means the candidate's habit is exactly the one the reset moved away from.
- No advance on a 2 in row 2 (Judgment about not promising product). Drift toward future-state selling is the failure mode the search was reset to avoid.
- No advance on a 2 in row 5 (Stage fit) without an explicit written note that we are deliberately changing the brief — i.e. owning the scope change instead of letting the hire change it.
- A stronger candidate who does not fit the brief is not the right hire. A weaker candidate who fits the brief is. This is the rule that keeps the search from quietly redefining itself by who showed up.
- "We picked the safer candidate" is not an acceptable internal reframe. If the chosen candidate is the fit, say it is because they match the reset brief — not because the other finalist was weak.
- Generic executive-impression language is not a substitute for the rows above. "Polished," "high presence," "strong communicator" do not score any row.

KEEP-LIST FOR INTERVIEWERS (the early call should produce evidence against these)
- Asks what design-partner learning currently lives in people's heads vs. docs vs. product telemetry.
- Separates activation friction from broader expansion / commercial / procurement noise.
- Distinguishes packaging/clarity work from true roadmap commitments without being evasive.
- Names where customer-growth owns vs. where founder / product / commercial owners stay in the lane.
- Asks for minimum viable evidence rather than a fantasy dashboard.
- Comfortable that some chaos is part of the job; not allergic to direct customer work herself.

AVOID-LIST FOR INTERVIEWERS (do not let the early call drift into these)
- Hypothetical feature-date negotiation.
- "How would you close this one enterprise logo no matter what?" prompts.
- Open-ended territory / pipeline / comp-plan questions that imply we are hiring a conventional VP Sales.
- Anything that invites bespoke roadmap promises for Evergreen-style accounts.
- Lighthouse-logo framing presented as the primary customer-growth outcome.
- Org-chart-heavy first-90-day language as the answer to ambiguity.
- Promises — explicit or implied — about SSO timing, audit history, admin-vs-billing-owner separation, or a procurement packet shipping on any timeline.

WHAT THIS TEMPLATE DOES NOT ANSWER
- Whether the candidate is the right external face while founders are still in the room (probed in references).
- Whether they can manufacture enough process without overbuilding (probed in the first-build scenario).
- Whether they prioritize well when packaging fixes and real product gaps sit in the same backlog (probed in the mixed-evidence scenario).
These go to the finalist loop, not the early call.

OPERATING NOTE
The five rows above are the comparison frame agreed for early calls. Finalist packets use the same five rows as the evidence base; the finalist loop adds scenario-based probing on top. Do not invent a sixth row for the early call — if the call surfaces something the rows do not cover, write it under Notes / Flags and raise it explicitly, do not retrofit the rubric.

input.body:
Recollection, written 2026-09-14, of how I sized up Marcus's early on-call work back in January 2023.

Context: Marcus had been on the team only a short while when the January 20, 2023 one-on-one landed. The on-call rotation was still rough — the support-rotation document was still on my January 10 follow-up list that week, and the system had a recurring 2 a.m. pager mistake that nobody had clean ownership of.

What he did in that 1:1:
- Dug into the handoff gaps in the on-call rotation on his own, past what I had asked for.
- Traced the recurring 2 a.m. pager mistake to a root cause rather than treating it as a one-off.
- A few days later, on January 24, he sent an FYI about a new deploy approval gate he had put in place — not a request for permission, just a heads-up that the control existed.

My read at the time: that deeper-than-asked investigation was the signal he was settling in. Not just executing the rotation, but trying to make the rotation less bad for the next person. The deploy-approval FYI reinforced it — he was tightening the system around his own work without being prompted.

Why I'm writing this down now (Sep 2026): three and a half years on, the pattern still matches. The judgment I made in that January 2023 1:1 — that Marcus was the kind of engineer who would rather fix the rotation than survive it — has held up. Worth keeping as a reference point when I'm calibrating newer hires against the same signal: do they go one layer deeper than asked, and do they close the loop without being chased?

input.body:
Historical Analysis Brief
Subject: Retention investigation wanted after the February 13, 2023 lead-partner meeting
Recorded: September 14, 2026 (historical reconstruction)

1. Context of the meeting
- February 13, 2023, 11:00 a.m. Pacific; lead-investor partner meeting.
- Meeting concluded by evening; overall tone was reasonable and the room felt fine.
- Morgan half-answered or hand-waved two pointed retention questions from the partner.

2. What the partner pressed on
- Question A: month-12 retention.
- Question B: a second, unrecorded retention question that was not cleanly fielded.
- The hand-waving on these two is the trigger for the investigation, not the meeting tone itself.

3. Why this was the main risk
- Month-12 retention is the dominant risk because the youngest cohort with month-12 data is the one with >=6 months of tenure as of the meeting; cohorts newer than that cannot answer month-12 yet.
- Any honest answer required either restricting to the mature cohort or showing a fixed-maturity curve, not a naive blended number.

4. Retention investigation I wanted to run after the meeting
- Build the lead dataset as the cleaned CSV, not Mixpanel, so the exclusions and rationale are auditable.
- Pre-write the fixed-maturity cohort curve (cohort defined by start month, retention measured at the same maturity for every cohort) so month-12 can be read off without cohort-immaturity bias.
- Document, line by line, each exclusion in the CSV: who was excluded, on what basis, and why the exclusion does not change the headline number.
- Stage a defense of the month-12 figure for any cohort-immaturity pushback: which cohorts contribute, which do not, and why the answer is still defensible.
- Have the rationale one click away from the deck so the partner questions can be re-answered cold, without Morgan re-deriving in the room.

5. What this brief is
- A historical record of the retention investigation I wanted to initiate after 2/13/2023.
- It captures intent and structure, not completion status; treat follow-through as a separate workstream.

6. Open questions for the actual workstream
- Who owns the cleaned CSV refresh cadence.
- Where the fixed-maturity curve lives (deck appendix vs. standalone model).
- Whether the second partner question (B) is recoverable from notes, or whether it has to be reconstructed from the deck page that prompted it.

Historical note — early April 2023, API v1 billing and inbound-event routes

This is a frozen historical record. It describes what was true on the Scaffold
API v1 surface during early April 2023. Nothing here is current guidance. Do
not infer that any route, endpoint shape, authentication scheme, or rate-limit
behavior described below is still in effect.

Period covered: ~April 6 – April 14, 2023.

Billing integration (billing setup, connected to API v1)
- On April 6, 2023, API v1 was connected to the new billing setup.
- On April 6, 2023, the working billing endpoints were /charges and /refunds.
- Authentication for the billing integration used the basic-auth token that had
  been created during the previous sprint.

Inbound-event route (webhooks, receiving inbound events)
- On April 8, 2023, POST /v1/webhooks was added to the API for receiving
  inbound events.
- That same morning (April 8, 2023), work was focused on webhook retry logic,
  including an exponential-backoff fix. After the fix, webhook retries stopped
  piling up unexpectedly.

Rate limiting (as observed on April 12, 2023)
- API v1 had a 100-requests-per-minute cap on its basic-auth tier.
- Inbound webhook traffic shared the same basic-auth rate-limit bucket as the
  rest of the API.

Authentication transition
- As of April 14, 2023, the API used JWT authentication.

Notes on framing
- This document intentionally mixes details from different days in the early
  April 2023 window. Each item is dated in-line so the chronology is preserved.
- This is not a migration guide and does not describe current route names,
  auth schemes, or rate limits. Later changes (including the move to JWT and
  any later auth/limit revisions) are out of scope for this note.
- Anything that is not explicitly listed above was not asserted from the
  underlying records and should not be back-filled into this note.

Auth Rewrite — October 2023 Cleanup Plan

Context: Following the auth migration rollout, residual scaffolding remains in the codebase and customer-facing channels. This plan captures the staging toggles, rollback flag, and release announcement cleanup as it was scoped in October 2023.

Staging toggles
- Inventory remaining feature flags tied to the auth rewrite in staging configs.
- Confirm each flag has a documented default and owner.
- Remove flags that have been at 100% for two consecutive release cycles.
- Keep kill-switch flags until the cleanup milestone closes.

Rollback flag
- Verify the auth rollback flag is wired to both API and worker entrypoints.
- Confirm rollback restores the prior session-validation path without data migration.
- Document the exact operator steps (flag name, expected propagation time, validation checks).
- Test rollback once in staging before the cleanup window closes.

Release announcement
- Draft the customer-facing note covering: what changed, what stayed the same, required customer action (none expected), and support contact.
- Stage the announcement for the auth GA date; align with the rollback flag docs above.
- Have support pre-briefed with the top three anticipated questions and answers.
- Archive the final sent announcement alongside this deck for historical reference.

Historical context only. Mercury is closed as a product (setup/support-quality lane). This note captures how UI decisions and release-readiness calls were owned while Mercury was live, so spot QA and any cleanup work stays bounded.

Scope of this document
- What Mercury UI was: the customer-facing admin/workspace surfaces built on top of Mercury's setup-and-support plumbing.
- Who owned what during active development.
- Where decisions belonged.
- How disagreements were resolved.
- What is still in scope (spot QA on existing surfaces) and what is NOT (new Mercury product work, staffing, roadmap).

Lane reminder (do not reopen)
- Mercury = setup/support-quality only.
- 7/24 cleanup pass: DONE.
- Going forward: spot QA on already-shipped Mercury surfaces only.
- Never: new Mercury product, new Mercury features, Mercury staffing, Mercury roadmap.
- The Mercury admin audit CSV is INPUT only - used for spot QA triage, never as a brief for new work.

1. Design owners (Mercury UI, historical)
- Product design lead (Mercury): owned UI direction, interaction patterns, and the design system tokens used by Mercury surfaces. Final say on visual + interaction decisions within the Mercury admin/workspace scope.
- Frontend engineering lead (Mercury): owned implementation feasibility, component reuse from the shared design system, and shipping sequencing. Signed off that a design could be built without bespoke infra.
- Mercury PM (Morgan, with Devon on commercial/procurement angles): owned scope. Defined what shipped vs. what was deferred, and what was explicitly out of scope.
- Customer support lead: surfaced UX issues from tickets and feed them back to design + frontend as inputs, not decisions.

2. Release-readiness owners
- Release captain (rotating, frontend eng lead by default): owned the release checklist, the go/no-go call, and the rollback plan. Could hold a release for any unresolved Sev-1/2.
- QA lead: owned test coverage sign-off and the spot-QA bar on already-shipped surfaces.
- On-call SRE: owned the deploy, monitoring during rollout, and the rollback execution if called.
- PM (Morgan): owned scope sign-off (what is in this release) and the customer-facing note if behavior changed. PM did not own the technical go/no-go.

3. Where decisions belonged
- Visual / interaction design: Mercury design lead, with frontend eng confirming buildability.
- Scope (what is in or out of a release): PM.
- Technical architecture and component reuse: frontend eng lead, with design lead consulted when reuse affected look/feel.
- Ship / no-ship: release captain, with PM holding scope and QA holding coverage.
- Customer messaging on a release: PM.
- Incident response during rollout: on-call SRE, with PM notified.

4. How disagreements were resolved
- Design vs. engineering (buildability): frontend eng lead writes up the constraint (cost, perf, component gap) in one paragraph. Design lead responds in one paragraph with the user-facing reason the design exists. If still unresolved, release captain picks the option that ships on time with the smallest user-visible regression, and the deferred item is filed (not relitigated in-thread).
- PM vs. engineering (scope vs. effort): PM holds scope. Engineering writes up the effort delta. If the effort delta blocks the release window, the item is cut from this release, not descoped silently. Cuts go in the release note.
- Release captain vs. anyone on go/no-go: release captain decides. Dissent is recorded in the release doc, not overridden.
- Cross-team (Mercury vs. another product surface): the other product's lead and the Mercury design lead each write one paragraph. PM (Morgan) breaks the tie. The break is final for that release; the underlying question is parked for the next planning round.
- Repeated unresolved disagreement on the same question: it becomes a written decision in the Mercury decision log, owned by PM, with the date and the rationale. Reopening requires a new fact, not a new opinion.

5. Spot QA lane (current, post-cleanup)
- Inputs: admin audit CSV, support tickets tagged Mercury-UI, on-call flags.
- Owners: QA lead triages; frontend eng lead fixes only what is broken on already-shipped surfaces; PM confirms the fix is in the spot-QA lane and not a new feature.
- Decisions: QA lead owns the triage call (fix now / watch / close). PM owns the lane-boundary call (this is QA, not new product work).
- Disagreement on whether something is "broken on a shipped surface" vs. "new Mercury product": PM decides. Default is: if the requested change adds behavior not present at ship time, it is new product and out of scope.

6. Out of scope (do not reopen via this handoff)
- New Mercury features, redesigns, or product bets.
- Mercury staffing changes.
- Mercury roadmap or reliability-roadmap commitments.
- Using the admin audit CSV as a brief for new work.

7. Pointers
- Mercury decision log: historical record of resolved disagreements.
- 7/24 cleanup pass doc: what was closed and what was deliberately left alone.
- Admin audit CSV: input for spot QA only.

End of handoff. Treat as historical context. Do not extend Mercury's surface area based on this note.
